On this matter of pipe lines, Mr. Speaker, let me make the position abundantly clear again. We have done so before, but for the record I repeat that we in this party have supported the construction of the pipe line from Alberta to eastern Canada. We were the first party to support the construction of that line by an all-Canadian route. Indeed it took us two years to convert the Minister of Trade and Commerce and persuade him to accept the idea of an all-Canadian route.
The franchise was given to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines on two promises, first, that they could finance the construction without government aid, and, second, that they would build into eastern Canada and deliver gas there before delivering it into the United States. That later was modified to make it simultaneous. However, the basis was that they were not to put gas into the United States before they put it into eastern Canada.
Here we are in 1956. What of their performance? Not one inch of pipe has been laid. The company says it has no finances with which to construct the line. Yes, these companies backing this Trans-Canada Pipe Lines company, which have billions of dollars of assets, say they cannot finance this construction. These people cannot or will not build the easiest portion of the line across

the prairies. Theirs is a record of default. That default has been overlooked and forgiven by the government. How forgiving they have been! When I asked the Prime Minister last week what would happen if and when default occurs next April, he could not tell me what the government would do. In the light of their record I think they can be expected to overlook that default also.
Mr. Speaker, here is a government which, in the face of default, has taken no action. Has it thrown open to others the opportunity to come in and bid on a project of this kind, and show what they were prepared to do? No; the Minister of Trade and Commerce, with his big stick, has frightened off all others. The government three months ago decided to relieve this company of the burden of constructing the 675-mile line across northern Ontario from the Manitoba boundary to Kap-uskasing. As if that were not enough, they are now going to finance the construction of the easiest leg of the line.
There we have this hybrid scheme, part public ownership. In fact all that is to be done is to be done by public assistance. We will have two portions which will not be connected, and we have no assurance that they will be connected or that a line will be constructed from Kapuskasing to the market in eastern Canada. Now the money to build that line in western Canada is to be taken from the crown corporation that was to build the line in northern Ontario, thereby depriving that corporation, to the extent of $80 million, of the capital needed for construction in northern Ontario, and thus delaying it. Let some of the hon. members from northern Ontario stand up and acknowledge that fact before their constituents. Yes; that is true.
For whom does the government of Canada turn somersaults and produce these favors? A company that is owned and controlled 83 per cent by United States capital, not by small United States investors, but by big interests quite capable of looking after themselves; and all through the piece Canadians have been driven off. We do not know how many others would have come forward if they had not been afraid of the big stick of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Mr. Speaker, the government tries to defend this as an example of free enterprise. What free enterprise is left in this Trans-Canada Pipe Line? This rugged mileage in northern Ontario is to be built by a crown corporation at the expense of all the taxpayers of Canada. The easiest part of the line, in western Canada, is to be built to the extent of $80 million, at the expense of the people of Canada. That is not my idea of free enterprise at all. I will tell you what explains this phenomenon. It could not be explained otherwise in a country that cherishes democracy even when this government has betrayed it. There are three instances that will explain what has happened. The first occurred in 1911, a great year in Canadian history. The Conservatives in that year in this House of Commons blocked the reciprocity bill by a prolonged discussion. This government did not want a repetition of 1911. They did not want prolonged discussion even on a measure as important as anything that has come before this House of Commons since 1911.
Then in 1955 there was the debate on the iniquitous demand of the government for a continuance of the absolute powers contained in the Defence Production Act. We defeated that iniquitous demand for absolute powers because we were able to keep this debate going long enough to arouse the country. When the country saw the issue at stake, its response was clear and definite and the Prime Minister had to capitulate. It is a repetition of that which this government is seeking to avoid now by the application of this iniquitous closure.
From that time to this, the defeat inflicted by democracy and the working of parliamentary methods upon the Minister of Trade and Commerce has rankled with him, and he has been looking for the first opportunity to settle accounts with the Canadian House of Commons. He is doing it now because the government has kowtowed to him, as have all hon. members opposite.
Finally there is a third explanation. You can find it associated with the one-man ruler in that speech he made at the opening of this session, when he called upon Liberal members in this house and the other place to toe the party line. This is the man who said, "If we wanted to get away with it, who would stop us?" Well, the majority could have, but they submitted weakly. I apply those words of Shakespeare, "O calm, dishonourable, vile submission!"
There is nothing more favourable to be said for the Social Credit group in this house. They have been the willing accomplices of the government all the way through. There have been to date in this debate 60 divisions, and the Social Credit group has been with the government on 59 of those. Of the eight closure motions to stifle debate and deprive members of this house of their democratic


rights, to prevent them from discharging their, responsibilities, the Social Credit group has voted with the government on all but the very first. Their batting average is something over 98 per cent with the government on this issue. I say they have forfeited all claim to understand and defend the freedom of parliament.
I have said before that this government has no mandate to do what it is doing. In the face of the pretext the Prime Minister has given the house for not taking this issue to the sovereign electorate of Canada, I say that the real reason and the only reason that prevents the people of Canada today from having the opportunity of passing on this issue that is their right is cowardice on the part of the government, moral cowardice. This parliament has been discredited by all that has happened. All sense of respect on the part of the people of Canada has gone. It has been destroyed by the actions of this government.
Sir, our policy was explained in full detail last night by my leader. In the amendment he has put before the house, we asked for consideration of this matter at various stages.
I understand that I have just two minutes left. We are now in the very final stage of the situation in which the government has put us, the third reading. Only a few hours of debate remain. We have been deprived of the opportunity we should have had in the interests of all the people of Canada to put this issue before the searching inquiry of a committee of the house, and to give others an opportunity to put forward their proposals. Well, sir, it seems now we are narrowed down to a choice between two courses, the government's iniquitous proposal to hand over to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited great sums of public money to help them out and public construction of the entire line. We choose the latter.

We say that the bill before the house for third reading may not be perfect; it may not represent the best plan for providing a satisfactory market, but it is a good bill and it does provide a pipe line into which we can turn the gas that is now going to waste, and we shall vote for third reading of the bill for these reasons.
In the first place, Mr. Speaker, we decry waste of any kind, and especially waste of a valuable product of our resources. At the present time, and for a long time, there has been great waste of this valuable fuel in Alberta owing to the fact that it is the lifting power for oil. In our efforts to produce
4696	HOUSE OF
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation oil to try to make Canada as self-sufficient as we can we have had to bring gas to the surface for which we can find no use, at least for some of it. There is, and will be, a greater waste as the days go by if we attempt to increase the production of oil, try to step it up. We do not want to see that. When a pipe line is built the waste can very largely be stopped and oil production can be stepped up without wasting the gas. That is one of the great reasons why there is urgency for the provision of a pipe line.
The second important reason why we support the pipe-line bill is that we are anxious to see our country's economy strengthened by the widest possible development of our resources. We have in Alberta huge gas reserves. Indeed, we are on the verge of very large further exploration programs that will undoubtedly result in the discovery of more reserves, and if we can find a market for the gas soon there is no doubt in my mind that we shall be able to increase the visible reserves by not less than a trillion feet a year for the next 10 or 15 years, and that means money in circulation; it means a stabilizing influence on our economy; it means more employment, and it will strengthen the economy of the whole of Canada.
It also means, Mr. Speaker, the development of a petrochemical industry in our province. It is not generally recognized that we do not just take the natural gas out of the ground, turn it into a pipe line and send it to a market in the east or in the United States. What is done is to put it through a separation plant and take out of it everything but the methane. It is only methane that goes into the pipe line. Butane, propane, sulphur and all these other things are taken out of it. They are left in the province and there they contribute to the development of a petrochemical industry. There is a $100 million industry waiting to get under way that cannot get under way until we find sufficient markets for the methane to make it possible for us to produce the by-products, to separate them from the gas and use them in a petrochemical industry in the province.
Is it not conceivable, therefore, and is it not a point of logic, to say that with a pipe line supplying the gas to a satisfactory market in eastern Canada and in the United States we would be able to strengthen the economy of Canada greatly through the development of a petrochemical industry in the province of Alberta? For years we have been short of sulphur; for years we have been on the verge of having to shut down a good many of our paper plants because of the fact that


we did not have enough sulphur. It looks to me as though we ought to be doing everything we possibly can to increase the production of that very valuable chemical and see that it is made available to our Canadian industry. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, those are important things to keep in mind.
Not only that, but the minister and others have already pointed out that there are serious fuel shortages expected in certain provinces of Canada. Manitoba is one of them. They experienced a serious shortage last year, and they expect one this year unless something is done to provide them with a supply of gas. There is a shortage in Ontario. Something has to be done here. If we can get the pipe line built and gas coming into northern Ontario it will give a tremendous impetus to resources development in the northern part of this province, that simply cannot go on unless they get this source of fuel.
Another important point that ought to be kept in mind, Mr. Speaker, is that the sooner we can get the gas through the pipe line and into the markets of eastern Canada and the United States the sooner will it be possible for us to begin a substantial saving of United States dollars that now go to buy United States fuel to be brought in to this country. That in itself is of tremendous value to us, and helps every part of our economy. That argument should appeal especially to the logical mind because of the very serious imbalance of trade we have with the United States today. Every single dollar we can save helps us that much. Every dollar's worth of gas we can export into that country will help to close the imbalance by that much.
We are not afraid, Mr. Speaker, that our natural gas resources will fall under the control of United States buccaneers, as they have so often been called. Let me point out once again what both the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance have so well said before. I should not have to say it at all, but it appears we have just to keep repeating these things to drive them home to some people who do not want to see the truth.
The fact is that this gas does not belong to the federal government at all. That gas belongs to the people of the province of Alberta. That gas could be brought out of the ground and used internally in Alberta without the consent of this government and without asking for any help at all.
The people of the province of Alberta have set up a natural gas conservation board which has complete control of the supply of gas and the allocation of that gas anywhere within or without the province. When I say "without the province" I refer to export.

That board can close oft the supply of gas it they feel that control is being taken away from us by some other country. I have had sufficient experience with the natural gas conservation board to be able to stand here and on my responsibility assert that they will never allow that important resource to come under the control of any United States buccaneers or anybody else outside Canada. My hon. friends ought to know that.
The Leader of the Opposition, for whom I have high regard, has repeated time and again during this debate-I should not dignify it by calling it a debate; during the discussion of this bill and the agreement with Trans-Canada Pipe Lines-the statement that we are wantonly transferring control of valued resources to a company 83 per cent of which is owned in the United States. That is not so, and no one can bring detailed evidence to prove that it is so.
Let me quickly assert the facts connected with it, and I am sure my hon. friend will recognize the truth of what I say. The partners in this venture, that is the partners in its beginning, in its organization, are Canadian Gulf, which owns vast resources of gas in the province of Alberta and which is owned by British American, a fairly large portion of which is held by Canadian shareholders. Then there is Canadian Delhi, and there are a large group of Canadian shareholders in that company. There is Tennessee Gas and Canadian Hudson Bay, a large portion of which is held in Canada.
Those who have fully investigated this matter assert that not less than 25 per cent of the equity capital already provided is owned by Canadians. I am talking about the equity capital which is the capital put up by the partners for the purpose of getting the company organized and under way and upon which the financing of the future is based. That is the only part of it about which it can truthfully be said the majority is held in the United States.
When financing is completed we hope that fully 60 per cent or more of the company will be Canadian-owned. Let me tell you that the Canadian people will have that opportunity; if they have venture in their souls, if they want to risk some capital they will have a chance to own and control 60 per cent or more of this company. If they do not take advantage of it that will be the fault of the Canadian people themselves. Notwithstanding anything the opposition has said, it is not true to say that the company is owned 83 per cent by Americans.

Mr. Speaker, from the very outset of this debate considerable attention has been paid to one issue, perhaps more than to the pipe line itself;
I refer to the question of parliamentary rights.
I feel that sufficient has been said by hon. members on this side of the house with respect to the government's conduct during this debate, but I should like to make brief reference to the role of the government supporter or backbencher during the course of the pipe-line debate in parliament. I noted an article in the Toronto Telegram of Monday, June 4, entitled "They Let the Boom Down" by Judith Robinson. The first paragraph of this reads:
Epitaph on a free parliament. The Liberal member for Qu'Appelle, Saskatchewan, was on the first plane out of Ottawa, Saturday morning. Going home for the week end, he said. Back on Monday to vote the pipe line through. He laughed. "No more horsin' around with rules," he said. "We fixed that. Kickin' us around. That's what they were doin' and we'd had enough of it."
"We don't hafta take it, see?" the Liberal member for Qu'Appelle, Mr. Mang, M.P., said, "and we aren't gonta."
"So we decided we'd let the boom down on them yesterday and that's what we did."
"We let the boom down and we let it down in a big way. See?"
I think that pretty well typifies the attitude of government supporters, including the "socred" supporters of the government, throughout the course of this debate. They have applauded every motion of closure and have tried to howl down every speaker of the opposition who said anything uncomplimentary about this bill or the way the government was railroading it through parliament.
This particular private member is quite proud of himself because the boom was lowered. I suggest that the hon. member had nothing to do with lowering any boom. The government decided when the boom was going to be lowered. I think the average government backbencher is as ill-informed about what the government proposes to do as any member in the opposition.
It is not only the member for Qu'Appelle who has made certain statements in this house which do not bear very close examination. The hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart), speaking the other day, as recorded on page 4604 of Hansard, had this to say. I draw to your attention that he was referring to a debate on agricultural problems in Canada. He said:
That is why I am suggesting tonight I only wish that we had used closure before, and I hope we use it more often in the future.
I think that statement offers a warning to the farmers of this country that they may


expect any time agriculture is going to be discussed-and I feel certain that the hon. member for Charlotte was typical of the Liberals of this house-he is going to demand and expect that closure be used to choke off any discussion on agriculture. During the course of this session we have had several important debates. I think the great wheat debate earlier in the session was of extreme importance to the welfare of this country, as is, of course, the question of the pipe line. Yet when the government is so unsure of itself and so anxious to hide the details of legislation that it will use closure at every step in order to choke off discussion, then I submit that what the hon. member for Charlotte has said may well be taken as warning. That is why I feel that the battle being put up by the opposition in this house against the government procedure is extremely important for the future of parliament.
There have been other comments, but I do not want to take up the time of the house in referring to them. One of the Toronto members, as recorded on page 4597, used smear tactics. We are more or less accustomed to hearing these from the "socreds", but it is a little distasteful to hear smear tactics coming from the mouths of the so-called Liberals, although this debate has indicated quite clearly that there is not a shred of Liberalism on the other side of the house or they would rebel against the authoritarian measures used by this government to ram the bill through the house.
There has been talk about haste. I have had occasion to look through Hansard for the past few years, looking through the debates on the address and the budget debates and various other debates in parliament. I do not recall any member of the "socred" group demanding that the government get on with the pipe line. I do not recall any Liberal shedding crocodile tears about the wastage of gas in Alberta. I challenge any member of the "socred" group to state when he at any time in the past two years has insisted on the building of this pipe line. They sat by and did nothing until the chosen instrument of both the Manning government and this government had received from the government all they had asked for.
Last summer the Minister of Trade and Commerce went out to Calgary. He and his officials met the representatives of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited. At that time he agreed on behalf of the taxpayers of Canada to build the northern Ontario section of the pipe line. One might have thought then that Trans-Canada Pipe Lines would have been prepared to go ahead with the project. No;

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation
they wanted a still bigger hand-out from the taxpayers, and so they stalled around.
We know full well what happened. It was only when the government had not only promised to build a pipe line across northern Ontario but in addition had offered to provide $80 million of the taxpayers' money for their purposes that they suddenly decided they were going to go ahead and start this year on the pipe line. We have been waiting for Trans-Canada Pipe Lines to go ahead for over five years. The "socreds" have been sitting by and doing nothing about it. The government supporters have been sitting by and have not criticized Trans-Canada Pipe Lines. However, as soon as Trans-Canada Pipe Lines feels it has got enough out of the taxpayers of this country so it will go ahead, the Minister of Trade and Commerce says, "This is going to go through by June 7 or else". That is the background behind the distasteful scenes we have witnessed in this house in the past few weeks, and all of it can be laid squarely on the doorstep of this government.
In the course of the debate we have offered alternative proposals. I think the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn), stated about a week ago that the premier of Saskatchewan had been silent. I wish to refer him and hon. members who support the government on that side of the house to a copy of the sessional paper brought down on February 21, which contains correspondence between this government and various provincial premiers. At that time the premier of Saskatchewan, in writing to the Prime Minister, pointed out this. I am not going to take the time to read the entire letter. Closure is in effect, and I must move along very quickly:
Like many other Canadians I am profoundly disturbed at the turn of events in connection with the construction of the trans-Canada gas pipe line. It is becoming increasingly apparent that the control of a vital natural resource is destined to fall into the hands of financial interests outside of Canada. I do not think that the people of Canada will view with equanimity the fact that a function so important to our economic development as the transmission of natural gas will to a considerable extent have been alienated from their control. I am concerned lest posterity charge us with having failed for the want of a bold and imaginative program on natural gas transmission.
He goes on further:
In repeated public statements I have made it clear that the Saskatchewan government is of the opinion that the trans-Canada pipe line should be a public utility with the government of Canada building the main transmission line and the province involved building the lateral transmission lines. From press statements I gather that your government is opposed to such a policy. I would like to suggest that as an alternative you might sound out the provinces involved to see if they would be prepared to enter into an arrangement
with your government for the joint construction and operation of the trans-Canada pipe line.
Your government has already expressed its willingness to enter into an arrangement with the province of Ontario for the construction of the unprofitable portion of the line which runs through northern Ontario. It would seem to me that having accepted this much responsibility there are sound reasons for proceeding one step further and constructing the entire line as a publicly-owned utility. By doing this the people of Canada would retain control of a vital natural resource and would have power to direct its usage in such a manner as to best advance the interests of the Canadian economy.
That was the letter sent by the premier of Saskatchewan to the Prime Minister of Canada, dated November 29, 1955. The Prime Minister made a reply to that letter, in which he said:
I wish to acknowledge your letter of November 29, expressing your fears about the private ownership of the trans-Canada gas pipe line and suggesting a conference of representatives of this government and yours and the governments of Ontario, Quebec and Manitoba to create instead some sort of agency owned, financed and controlled by these five governments to establish and operate a gas pipe line from Alberta to Quebec.
As no doubt you are aware, my colleagues and I have no preference in principle for public ownership rather than private ownership in business and we are prepared to consider in any particular case whether, and to what degree, governmental participation in an enterprise is in the public interest. In this particular case we came to the conclusion that some temporary governmental participation was necessary in the national interest in order to get the project started.
I would draw to your attention that the Prime Minister's concluding paragraph reads as follows:
This matter will undoubtedly be the subject of discussion early in the next session of our parliament. In these circumstances, I feel it would be improper of me to attempt in correspondence with you to anticipate the substance of that discussion.
I have no doubt that the points you raise will come up in the debates in the House of Commons and those speaking for this government will be quite prepared to explain the reasons why a course of action of the type you suggest was not followed.
We have waited for that explanation. I have not heard the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance or any cabinet minister or any private member on the government side or any of the spokesmen of the "Socred" party give any reasons why the Prime Minister refused to entertain this reasonable proposal put forth by the premier of Saskatchewan. The Prime Minister never had the decency to write a letter to the premier of Ontario and the premier of Manitoba. He ignored the proposition completely.
Then the government come before parliament and say that the only way this can be done is through this enormous give-away program to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines. If the Prime Minister had the decency to send a letter to Mr. Frost and to Mr. Campbell, he

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation could find out what they thought about this proposal, of course the government has been trying to suggest that the Ontario government is solidly behind them, and of course we know that is not true. The Minister of National Health and Welfare made a 100 per cent political speech the other night in which he said that Mr. Frost had made the statement and Mr. Porter had made the statement that the Ontario government was 100 per cent behind the federal government's proposal, but I note that a statement by Premier Frost to the conference held in the King Edward hotel last Saturday, as reported in the Toronto Telegram of June 2, was as follows:
Premier Frost says his own feeling today is still what he has previously stated it to be, that the pipe line is the sort of public utility undertaking that lends itself to public enterprise construction, either by the dominion government alone or by the government together with the provincial governments involved. But for reasons of its own the dominion government doesn't feel it wants to build the line itself either to operate forever or to lease or sell later to private interests. We must leave it to the dominion government and parliament to decide which way they'll get it here. We've agreed to make our contribution towards making sure that it comes through Canada all the way.
But at no time did the premier of Ontario ever reject public ownership. He never had a chance to reject it. The federal government did not make a proposal to the Ontario government that they enter into some sort of agreement to build the whole trans-Canada pipe line as a public undertaking. Oh, no; they simply went to the government of Ontario and said, "This is it, this is our chosen instrument, Trans-Canada Pipe Lines. We are not concerned about your wishes at all. If you want gas it is going to be through Trans-Canada Pipe Lines or not at all." The province of Ontario was put in the position where it was forced to accept the second best proposal, the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines proposal.
I should have thought that the Prime Minister of Canada would have had the common decency to seek the opinion of the provincial premiers; but when my colleague the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough) asked the Prime Minister a few days ago whether anything had been done respecting Mr. Douglas' suggestion that the provincial governments concerned might be consulted with a view to some sort of agreement whereby the line could be built as a public undertaking, the Prime Minister said that nothing had been done. He had not made any proposals to the provincial premiers. The government simply laid it on the line. They said, "This is it, Trans-Canada Pipe Lines. This is our baby, and if you want gas through northern Ontario you are going to have to take our proposal or nothing at all."


I think the statement of Premier Frost is quite clear and indicates that two provinces, without ever having been asked by the government, are already on record as being 100 per cent in support of a proposal to build the trans-Canada pipe line as a public utility. Yet this government is completely blind to the realities of the situation and tries to create the impression that the provinces are not concerned. Neither the Prime Minister nor any member of his cabinet has ever said a word about the proposal made by premier Douglas. They have completely ignored it, and the people of Canada will of course be the losers as the result of this transaction.
Why should the province of Ontario not be favourably disposed toward public ownership? I suggest that the Clarkson, Gordon report makes it abundantly clear that under private enterprise they would have to depend on exports of gas to the United States in order to make it feasible. But the same report indicates that even without the export of gas to the United States the project would be economically feasible under public ownership.
That was a report prepared for the Ontario government. Yet the federal government has chosen to ignore this report, has chosen to ignore the recommendation of the premier of Saskatchewan, and has determined to go its own blind way selling out the interests of the people of Canada for the benefit of a corporation, ownership of which lies to the south of the border
I suggest that throughout the course of the debate the Minister of Trade and Commerce has made government policy quite clear. He has stated in effect that if the job can be done by private enterprise, then private enterprise should be allowed to go ahead and do it. That means, of course, that if private enterprise figure there is enough profit they will go ahead and do the job. If, on the other hand, private enterprise does not do the job then the government will step in. What the government proposes to do in the present case is to have the taxpayers of Canada put up the risk capital. If the undertaking turns out to be profitable they will then turn over the project to private enterprise on extremely reasonable terms. If it is not' profitable, then the public will have a white elephant on their hands. That is government policy.
There has been a great deal of talk about the alienation of natural resources in this country. We know that the great iron ore resources of the province of Quebec are being sold to people outside this country by the Duplessis government at a cent a ton, but at least Duplessis did not put up any money. He did not put up taxpayers' money to allow

them to come in and exploit the resource. The pipe line is, after all, the important thing because gas capped in the well is of no value unless there is a pipe line, and in this instance the government is not only alienating this resource of Canada but is adding insult to injury by using the Canadian taxpayers' money to aid a foreign corporation to do the job. You know, it is bad enough when you allow a burglar to enter and rob your house, but when you turn around and give him the tools to do the job that is the essence of pure folly.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that throughout the course of this debate we have emphasized the importance of proceeding with this project. We have argued over the years that we ought to be enjoying this natural resource in this country and that the pipe line should have been built. The government has allowed the company concerned to procrastinate, to delay, to deceive parliament for over five years. Finally when the government get down on their hands and knees before the company and have given the company everything it wants and the company is apparently satisfied now that it is getting enough out of the Canadian taxpayers, this same company turns around and says to the government of Canada, "All right; you will put this through before the 7th of June or we may back out."
Why should Trans-Canada Pipe Lines want to back out? After all they have been given at the hands of the government why should they want to back out? But the solicitude for Trans-Canada Pipe Lines does not extend to other areas. We in Saskatchewan have been urging the government for many years to proceed with the South Saskatchewan dam, a project that is going to involve the expenditure of some federal money. But no; no money is available for the South Saskatchewan dam. As far as the maritime provinces are concerned, the government turns a deaf ear to the many needed projects down there.

Mr. Speaker, I seek the indulgence of the house at this final stage of this most vexatious debate in the hope that it may be possible for a few minutes, at least, for all of us to be stripped of political or party allegiance and to speak to each other not as politicians but as Canadians. I take this position because of the axiom that loyalty to our country transcends the loyalties we owe to political parties and no doubt supersedes all personal and political exigencies. I hold with Disraeli, who said:
First comes my God, then my Queen and country, then my party, then come I.

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation With this as a background let us analyse briefly the positions that have been taken by the respective parties in the house and some of the things that have been said by their spokesmen. First of all I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, that there are certain definite common denominators on which we all agree. Let us recognize these common denominators. Everyone in the house has agreed that a pipe line for Canada is vital, that a pipe line for Canada is needed, that a pipe line for Canada will help the future of our country. Of that there is no doubt. Not a single member of the house has stood up in his place to argue that the pipe line was not needed or would not be useful for our country. Hitherto, Mr. Speaker, members of the house were deluged with all forms of advice from the country when they opposed a project before parliament. We were accustomed to receiving briefs from chambers of commerce, submissions from boards of trade, petitions from labour unions, delegations, letters and telegrams. Not a word did anyone hear. There was no complaint from anybody. That told us clearly that not only the members of this house but the entire country without exception were in favour of having a pipe line constructed in Canada. Peculiarly enough, with this almost unanimous consent of the entire country, what has developed in this house? No one opposes it and yet this house was almost split in two and the country was almost split asunder on a matter on which we all agree. Peculiarly enough, as I said we seemed to differ on a very simple thing and that is the method of construction, the way it should be constructed.

I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the method of construction is not anything that should tear this parliament apart as it almost threatened to do. For example, let us examine what our socialist friends say as to how they would like to see the pipe line built. They say, "We would like a pipe line built, we are in favour of a pipe line, but we want it built our way, the socialistic way, publicly owned". I can understand that, Mr. Speaker. The socialists at least are consistent with their political philosophy. As they always do, they follow their teachers: Karl Marx, Robert Ingersoll and later Norman Thomas, Ramsay MacDonald and more lately Clement Attlee. It is a position to take, and I can understand it. But I put this question to my hon. friends. Are they socialists first or are they Canadians first? What would their answer be to that question if they were asked it? Would they sooner see no pipe line constructed at all if it could not be constructed

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation on socialistic lines? If they say yes, once they say that they favour the pipe line but would oppose it only on the ground that it is not built according to socialistic philosophy, they would be placing their socialism and their socialistic philosophy far above the interests of our country; and that is something they certainly should not do. Of course they cannot answer in that way.
It is true that the minister said at one stage that if there is default-and the hon. member who just took his seat repeated it- the government could take it over. Our socialist friends promptly shouted, "Why wait? Why not do it now?" The answer is also an obvious one. This government is not composed of Liberals in a hurry. We favour private enterprise and we have not yet reached the stage that the socialists have reached.
What do our friends of the Conservative party say? They too take the position that they want a pipe line but they say, "We are not in favour of public ownership; we are a private enterprise party". They have thrived through history because they were a private enterprise party. The government is trying to make of this a private enterprise. Why do they oppose it? They simply say, "We want a pipe line but we want it built our way". That is understandable. I can go along with it. They would like to see it built with Canadian money, under Canadian ownership and Canadian control. But I put this question to them. If a pipe line is so vital and so necessary for the country would they say, "No pipe line unless it can be built with Canadian money and Canadian ownership," assuming that what the government is doing does not give them that? I do not think that the Conservative party, with their loyalty to this country, can consistently say that they would prefer to have no pipe line rather than a pipe line built the way the government intends to do it.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, the Conservative party have been told as clearly and as categorically as possible that there is no other way, that there is no better way, by which a pipe line can be built now. They were told by the premier of the province of Ontario. They were told by this government. They were told by the man whom they themselves labelled as the one man in the house who knows more about gas pipe lines than anyone else here. He has told them. The premier of Ontario has told them. The premiers of the other provinces involved have told them. Yet they sit back almost doggedly, almost capriciously, and say, "We want a pipe line but we will not let you build it". They too

are in that predicament, Mr. Speaker. Their joining the socialist party is in my judgment a forceful denial of all their principles up to the present time. They seem to be bouncing from one foot to the other foot, making one manoeuvre or another manoeuvre as long as they can prevent the building of a pipe line. That conduct is not consistent with the welfare of our country. Perhaps there may be other motives which drive them into this course of action. Perhaps they have their eye on the next election in preference to the urgent needs of the country. If that is so, if it is true that they have their eye on the next election and, with that object in view, have created or helped to create the commotion in the house, let me say this to them. They fall directly into the category so magnificently enunciated by that great political thinker and cleric, the Abbe Raymal, who said this:
Politics in practice too often means all for party, nothing for people; all for office, nothing for honour; all for power, nothing for progress.
I can think of no more suitable description of the Conservative party if it is true-and I do not accuse them of this-that they have their eye on the next election in preference to having their eye on the well-being of the future of this country.
I also have another brief quotation. J. F. Clark, a recognized philosopher, said:
A politician looks for the success of his party; a statesman for that of his country.
I believe that the two hon. gentlemen, namely the leader of the C.C.F. party and the leader of the Conservative party, in really doing a little bit of soul-searching, will recognize that, once there is that universal agreement across the entire country that a pipe line should be built, they should, even at this late stage, give their views and their approach to this national problem a second look. Basically, Mr. Speaker, I believe that they are concerned with the well-being of this country above all else, but I believe that they have this entire picture in bad focus and are following a distorted line of action.
It is true, Mr. Speaker-and unfortunately so-that the debate on the bill has produced a by-product, namely the question of closure as it affects democratic rights. This too, Mr. Speaker, has been placed in very bad focus.
I submit that the country should be told, not in a rhetorical fashion but in the simplest language, that closure does not prevent debate. If debate was prevented, then it was prevented not by the government. Closure, in its real sense, was designed to fix a limit on the time of debate and nothing more.

We know now when the throne speech debate next year will be terminated. We know it now, we know it well in advance. Now, Mr. Speaker, there are two key questions upon which this whole matter revolves. The first is, why is this government building the northern Ontario section of the line for this company? This company received its franchise on the express understanding that it would complete the whole line unassisted by the government. Representatives of the company appeared before the board of transport commissioners on numerous occasions year after year and reaffirmed that assertion. Then, suddenly, the minister announced that the government is going to build this section of the line for the company. He made no explanation why the company is unwilling to live up to the undertaking on which it was awarded the franchise, and the company of course has said nothing on its own behalf. This is one of the great mysteries of the last few years.
It is obvious, I think, that the reason this government is building this section of the line for the company is that the wealthy United States interests which control Trans-Canada Pipe Lines have got the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) wrapped around their little finger. They have duped him into doing what they want him to do. Can you not see this whole thing taking place in the board room of one of the wealthy United States companies which own this Trans-Canada pipe line? You see the boys sitting around cutting up a melon in advance, and the talk, of course, gets around to the desirability of getting this government to build the northern Ontario section. But these businessmen, being men of common sense, realize that there is very little chance of being able to persuade the government to do this because they know that the government knows that among them they have several times the finances available to build this section. They know perfectly well that the government knows that they received the franchise on the express understanding that they would build the whole line unassisted, and also they know that their representatives have asserted time and again before the board of transport commissioners that this line would be built without financial assistance from the government. But it seems like an attractive idea, and it keeps coming back in the conversation and finally they decide, well, why not have a go at it; why not see if we can get in touch with C. D. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill now before the house unequivocally shows the importance which the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin) gives to the matter of bilingualism.
I heartily congratulate my colleague on this happy initiative and consider it an honour to have the privilege of supporting his efforts.
Outside of election time, when it is permissible to question the sincerity of those in office, our federal statesmen seldom have the opportunity to extend to minorities the benefits of their broad-mindedness, their understanding, and their generous impulses.
Now this pleasing opportunity is being offered to them by this bill. In fact it affords the government a wonderful chance to show French Canadians how much consideration it is prepared to give to their requests and how far they are willing to go in giving them a square deal.
The adoption or defeat of the bill will, to a large extent, reflect the pro-French or antiFrench sentiments of the leaders and supporters of the Liberal party.
There are things that should not have to be requested, and which, by their logic or nature, are self-evident necessities. Respect for and recognition of the two official languages of Canada are among them.
It might be assumed in certain quarters that in requesting bilingual cheques we are seeking a favour. The fact of the matter is that we are merely seeking confirmation, under a new form, of a sacred and inalienable right of the first settlers of this country.
The Acts of the Parliament of Canada and of the Legislature of Quebec shall be printed and published in both those languages.
So reads the final paragraph of section 133 of the British North America Act. It is the only constitutional document relating to bilingualism. Brief and concise, those few words, by their very ambiguity, have led to a restrictive interpretation of the principle stated, and this has been the basis of the unfortunate doctrine of the "Quebec Reserve . Faced with the French achievement, carried
Financial Administration Act out by a third of Canada's population, the Anglo-Saxon majority limited its concessions to the strict minimum in the federal field, leaving it to the province of Quebec to observe the letter and the spirit of the pact of 1867. However, the statement that no legal document protects the French language outside of Quebec is untrue. I am now quoting from chapter 3 of the Statutes of Canada 1870, 33 Victoria, section 23, admitting the province of Manitoba into confederation:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the houses of the legislature, and both those languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses; and either of those languages may be used by any person, or in any pleading or process, in or issuing from any court of Canada established under the British North America Act, 1867 or in or from all or any of the courts of the province. The acts of the legislature shall be printed and published in both those languages.
That section of the Manitoba Act implies that not only in the province of Quebec is the French language official. Therefore, the imperial act of 1848, which restored the official character of the French language in Upper and Lower Canada, also applied to the province of Ontario. The French-speaking delegates at the Quebec conference surrendered none of our rights.
Moreover, none were revoked by the imperial parliament.
In 1871, that parliament sanctioned legislation of vital importance. It was entitled "The British North America Act, 1871". It is chapter 28 of the Statutes of Victoria 34-35, assented to on June 29, 1871.
According to section 2 of that act, the federal parliament is empowered to form from time to time new provinces out of Rupert's Land and the Northwest Territories just acquired under confederation. I quote:
. . . and may at the time of such establishment make provision for the constitution and administration of any such province . . .
Now section 4:
The Parliament of Canada may from time to time make provision for the administration, peace, order, and good government of any territory not for the time being included in any province.
Section 5 confirms the two acts already voted by the federal parliament: the NorthWest Territories Act of 1869 and the Manitoba Act of 1870.
Section 6 provides that once the parliament of Canada has formed new provinces, it shall no longer have the right to alter the provisions of any law pertaining to them, save by prior agreement of the legislature concerned.

Without the slightest doubt, the source of most of the difficulties encountered by French Canadians in connection with the two official languages derives from the lack of clear and accurate definitions not only in the constitution itself but in the legislation enacted subsequently.

. The privileges we enjoy today in the exercise of some of our prerogatives have been more often conquered by us than generously granted by them.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PRINTING OF NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS IN BOTH ENGLISH AND FRENCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that as a Canadian of French descent, it is my duty to make a few comments concerning the bill that is now before this house. I think there is not much I can add to the remarks of the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin). His speech was a model of moderation, and indicates on the part of its author a thorough command of his subject.
I merely wish to add a few general thoughts and take this opportunity of making my position known on this important matter.
Financial Administration Act Quite a number of my supporters have asked me to state my position in this respect.
I have no hesitation whatsoever in stating that I support this bill with all my heart and that I will proudly vote in favour of its adoption.
The origin of bilingualism in Canada dates much farther back than 1867; the ^ French achievement is the very basis of the discovery and' colonization of our beautiful and great country. The hazards of European politics, in which we did not participate, ordained that we were to share with the Anglo-Saxon people the privilege of creating a young and vigorous nation.
This dual civilization, which enriches Canadian life and of which we are proud, must be exteriorized by all means of expression at our disposal.
Every people has its own character, its own genius, its own heredity. It might be thought by some people that we should not attach so much importance to the printing in both languages of government cheques and other negotiable notes. However, in my view, Mr. Speaker, it is a practical way of expressing the characteristics of the Canadian people.
The confederation act officially sanctioned the mutual wish of both racial groups of this country to work side by side for the greatness of Canada, in the respect of one another's rights.
The principle of bilingualism, Mr. Speaker, has been established and recognized by section 133 of the British North America Act. We should remember that section for it had a great influence all along the advance of the Canadian nation towards its maturity. It reads as follows:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the houses of the parliament of Canada and of the houses of the legislature of Quebec; and both those languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses; and either of those languages may be used by any person or in any pleading or process in or issuing from any court of Canada established under this act, and in or from all or any of the courts of Quebec.
The acts of the parliament of Canada and of the legislature of Quebec shall be printed and published in both those languages.
From the text I just quoted, it was obviously the legislator's intention to make the use of both languages mandatory in the drafting of official parliamentary documents. I admit that neither cheques nor other negotiable effects are specifically mentioned in clause 133, but if this section of the Constitution is to be construed practically and logically, the use of both official languages should obviously find place in every manifestation of Canadian life. In 1927, postal orders, money orders, postal and excise stamps were made
4710	HOUSE OF
Financial Administration Act bilingual. While this act of courtesy, of justice and generosity on the part of our Englishspeaking fellow citizens hurt no one, it was a great cause of satisfaction to all Canadians of French origin.
A second important step towards bilingualism was the issue of bilingual money in 1936. This took place under a Liberal government and the argument of those who held that this gesture might foster disagreement or create difficulties for the government is easily disproved by the fact that, since 1936, national unity has made giant strides, and the government that was responsible for it has been continually re-elected since.
The bill before us would complete the official recognition of bilingualism by printing in both languages cheques and other negotiable effects issued by the government or by a crown corporation. Once more our English-speaking compatriots are given a chance to show that they understand and appreciate the French element's share in the birth, conservation, safeguard and development of our country.
All through our political history, the Liberal party has been recognized as the party of Canadian unity. Its leaders have always given perfect examples of their broad-mindedness and of their spirit of conciliation. They have long since understood that Canada's future rests on the vitality of two great races having different traditions, marching side by side, but without merging or losing their characteristics and without there being any question of assimilation.
They also understood that each should strive to know the other better, and that while scrupulously respecting the constitutional rights of minorities, a study of both official languages should be encouraged as much as possible.
But to reach that goal, we must first recognize those languages in a practical and effective way everywhere in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, bilingual postage stamps, bilingual bank notes, bilingual cheques are all messages of good will that circulate between provinces. To foreigners they proclaim our bi-ethnical character, and to Canadians they testify to the maturity of our nation and effectively prove our mutual understanding and the reciprocal recognition of our mutual rights.
I do not want to speak too long, so as not to delay the passing of this bill.
In the past, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) has shown his spirit of fairness and understanding. I am confident he will grant


the request made in this bill and that he will give the necessary instructions so that, from now on, all cheques and negotiable instruments issued by the government or by crown corporations will be printed, as the bill says, both in English and in French.
Before 1 resume my seat, Mr. Speaker, let me say once again that I will be glad to vote in favour of the bill introduced by the hon. member for Beauce.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a true sense of pride that I rise now to give unconditional support to the bill under review, sponsored by my distinguished colleague, the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin).
When this bill was introduced, I hastened to congratulate the hon. member, and I take the new opportunity that is now offered me of congratulating him again most warmly, wishing with him that, in the interest of the great cause of the national unity of our country, this bill will become law as soon as possible.
Since I have been sitting in this house, I have noticed with very great satisfaction that our English-speaking compatriots, on both sides of the house and regardless of party, occasionally paid us the honour of using that other official language of Canada, which is my mother tongue.
We are grateful to them for their magnificent effort, and we hope that several others will follow their example. Thus the relations between the two great races which make up the majority in this country will be facilitated, and this can only lead to better understanding. The more Canadians who can fluently speak the country's two official languages, the more cordial our relations are bound to be and the more can we help cement for all time national unity, without which happiness and prosperity are impossible.
We should no longer have to be taught a lesson by great statesmen of the democratic world who honour us by their visits and who, unlike far too many Canadian members of parliament, address us in both official languages. I need quote no other examples than those of our gracious sovereign and of the Queen Mother, and last year that given by the President of the United States, Mr. Eisenhower, and more recently by the Prime Minister of Great Britain, Sir Anthony Eden, and this morning by the President of the Indonesian Republic, Mr. Sukarno.

If those great figures of the free world are pleased to address us in French and in English in the House of Commons, the debating hall of the representatives of the Canadian people, it is because they know and realize that there are in Canada two official languages, and that neither has precedence over the other, that they both have the same value and that they are both on an equal footing. As stated by previous speakers, my argument is based on the spirit of the Canadian constitution which recognizes bilingualism in our country.
Is it not true that in this very chamber, Mr. Speaker, you must use both languages, and are not our debates printed in both French and English?
There can therefore be no doubt that the two languages of Canada are officially recognized and no fair-minded Canadian would dare state the contrary.
This formula was vividly recognized-I may be allowed here, Mr. Speaker, to differ from the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Gauthier) who has just resumed his seat-by a Conservative administration under the late Right Hon. R. B. Bennett who, in deference to the wishes of the majority of Canadians and more particularly of the French-speaking Canadians, gave us bilingual money which, by the way, lost nothing of its value by reflecting the bilingual character of this country.
It never occurred to our Anglo-Saxon fellow citizens to refuse our country's money because it was printed in both languages.
It seems to me that, after such a forward step in the direction of common sense, even if more than 20 years have passed since that memorable day, we must continue on the road to progress, as far as bilingualism is concerned, by giving our unanimous approval to the bill introduced by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin).
In fact, the bill gives rise to no complication and, contrary to what the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) said, it entails no extra expenditure. In my view, the argument of the hon. minister is preposterous, and his more or less shaky explanation is but a pretext to reject the bill. I dare hope that, since he made that assertion, the hon. minister has revised his views, that he has undergone a complete change of mind and that he will gladly support the bill submitted to the approval of the house by the hon. member for Beauce.
Financial Administration Act
Those who print cheques, drafts, bills of exchange, postal notes, postal money orders and other negotiable instruments will not need more paper and will not charge more to the government for printing these documents in both languages, the more so since these documents are printed in millions of copies and that profits on such printing are very reasonable.
In adopting this bill, the government would show its patriotism and its understanding, and would greatly help to dissipate from the minds of my French-speaking compatriots their feeling of isolation in the province of Quebec.
The time has come to dispel from the minds of those who still cling to this antiquated view, the thought that the province of Quebec is a reservation where only French Canadians have access.
We want all Canadians, whatever their racial origin, to feel at home in the province of Quebec as long as they remain mindful of the law.
On the other hand, we want French Canadians, equally mindful of the laws in the other provinces of the confederation, to feel at home everywhere in Canada.
Why this distinction, why admit French in the province of Quebec and refuse it elsewhere? Yet there are more than a million French Canadians living in the rest of Canada. To my mind, this is a serious injustice which should be corrected in the shortest possible delay.
At this moment, all hon. members in this house are given a chance to show themselves as Canadians in the fullest sense of the word by voting without hesitation in favour of the bill presented by our distinguished colleague from Beauce.
In so doing, they will also rectify the injustice committed every day in the province of Quebec when English-speaking fellow-citizens receive cheques made out in French.
Let us act with justice and tolerance towards all, let us return to the spirit of the Canadian constitution and let us dedicate all our efforts to the making of a bilingual country of Canada.
All the speeches delivered on national unity will be but empty words if we cannot practise, at least in some measure, what we preach.
Mr. Speaker, with a few exceptions, all my electors are French-speaking and many of them have asked me to speak on their behalf on this occasion.

Financial Administration Act
I thank and congratulate from the bottom of my heart the hundreds of citizens of my riding who wrote to me about this matter. It shows that they consider this bill as important. However, I can assure them that, even without a word from them, I would have taken the same stand to demand without the least hesitation what I believe to be logical, fair and patriotic.
I want to congratulate particularly the management of the Paquet Company Limited of Quebec, the largest retail concern in our district, who took an interest in this bill and who acknowledge, even in the midst of a nearly 100 per cent French-speaking population, the necessity of bilingualism back home and everywhere in Canada. This example of true Canadianism should be followed throughout the country.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that every Canadian will appreciate the gesture of all those who, by word and vote, will support the bill which is now before the house and which I support myself with the utmost feeling, on behalf of all the people I represent here.
We are grateful to the hon. member for Beauce whose personal merit and well known patriotism make him a citizen of whom we are proud. He has acquired a new stature, if that were possible, in presenting this bill, and he has won the affection and the admiration of all who are worthy to be called Canadians.

On March 6 last, the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin) introduced for second reading Bill No. 149, entitled: An act to amend the Financial Administration Act. In language moderate and to the point, he explained to this house that the spirit of our constitution recognizes bilingualism in both the written and the spoken word. As a matter of fact, the existence of the French language in Canada has unquestionably affected the nature and the development of culture in this country.
In the last 25 years, and especially in the last decade, the constant growth of bilingualism in various parts of Canada is something which we could not help noticing. This development and progress have even had their effects in this house.
During the debate of the last few sessions, we have seen that a goodly number of mem-
[Mr. Dufresne.l
bers from predominantly or almost exclusively English-speaking communities have made it a point to say a few words in the other official language of Canada, and that they have expressed themselves in almost flawless French. This noble gesture on their part proves that they are ready to recognize the survival of the French language in Canada and the advantages of its constant growth as an instrument of culture in the various classes of society.
Indeed, Canada has its Canadian press which, although not always fully in agreement in the matter of ideas, has become an important factor of bilingualism and unity while reporting the national activities of the two main groups of our population. In our own press gallery, correspondents and reporters of both languages work side by side in a true brotherly spirit, in giving the people of this country their own interpretation of the proceedings in this house.
The desire for mutual understanding seems more and more evident among a large and growing number of our people, again as a means of maintaining, and of spreading if possible, the knowledge and the practical point of view of both languages in this country.
In 1936, the government of Canada unequivocally recognized the importance of, and the justification for, bilingualism in this country by giving our currency its present character. However, our money is not our sole means nor our sole aim in transactions. Cheques, in a general way, especially those issued by the federal government in the provision of social services, such as family allowances, old age pensions and others, as well as those which are regularly distributed to civil servants, should also carry that bilingual character which contributes to the solidarity and unity of our nation.
There is no doubt that bilingualism is growing, and is spreading to various areas of the country, without giving rise to undesirable controversy. The year 1955 has been memorable in the history of Canada, more particularly for the small Acadian people, who last year celebrated the second centennial of its deportation. Throughout Acadia, in numerous centres of the other Canadian provinces, in New England and in Louisiana celebrations marked the rebirth and survival of that small group who, exactly two centuries ago, were condemned to dispersal and near extinction. In New Brunswick alone that

small group now represents nearly 250,000 people, i.e. more than 40 per cent of the total population of the province. With its fellow citizens of British and other origins, it largely contributes to the fulfilment of their destiny on this American continent.
The granting of bilingual cheques by the federal government would be welcome, more particularly by New Brunswick, as a token of consideration and appreciation by those good people who offer a striking example of that understanding and co-operation which so largely contribute to the maintenance of our national unity.

I remember reading at that time the favourable comments in both the English and the French press, rejoicing over that decision of parliament. Since then, similar statements have been issued on many occasions. Newspapers and magazines have often printed statements of eminent people who earnestly asserted that cultural and racial duality in this country was of great advantage to the Canadian nation as a whole. Furthermore, as an hon. member who spoke before me was saying, we do not have to go back 20 years, 10 years, or even 5 years to find statements in favour of bilingualism in this country. We merely have to remember events that took place in this house since 1953, and particularly what was said by Queen Mother Elizabeth on the occasion of her visit, when in her splendid address delivered in both languages, she stated how privileged we were in Canada to have two official languages.
The President of the United States, Mr. Eisenhower, also made a similar statement in this house. We also heard the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, Sir Anthony Eden, express views to the same effect, in French and in English, and praise the extent of French culture in Canada.
The bill moved by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin) seeks no privilege nor favour. To my mind, his bill claims the recognition of a right. French-speaking Canadians living in all provinces of Canada are entitled, it seems to me, to have negotiable bills, issued by the federal government, printed in the two official languages of this country. Besides, as has already been pointed out, Frenchspeaking Canadians make up nearly one third
Financial Administration Act of the population of Canada, and in the province of Quebec itself that racial group is equal to 80 per cent of the population. Therefore, English-speaking Canadians enjoy preferential treatment in the province of Quebec, where the right to speak English is acknowledged by all, as it should be. On the other hand, French-speaking Canadians are at home everywhere in this country. That was brought home to me during a visit I made in western Canada, where I was happy to feel at home. That is why I am happy to note that from year to year French-speaking Canadians are more and more appreciated and liked. And this is pretty general. I know that in the past we heard statements to the effect that the French language was perhaps badly treated in certain quarters; today such statements do not hold any longer in this country. In the course of my research, going through files on bilingualism both in this house and elsewhere, I came across correspondence between a former member of this house, a Mr. Cohen, who was sitting here in 1936, and a young student in western Canada by the name of Boulanger. It has already been pointed out that we in Alberta have had the privilege of enjoying the use of gas as a fuel for a great number of years. However, in the part of the province which I am fortunate enough to represent, the development of gas and oil reserves has been a more recent thing. Just a few years ago it was our privilege in the small town in which I live to have gas introduced. I could speak at length on such gas fields as the Turner valley field, the Medicine Hat field, to which I believe the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) referred last night when he spoke of the gas fields as being over 40 years old, Kinsella, Viking, the Lloydminster, Vermilion and other fields. So far as I am concerned personally I do know that the development of gas and petroleum resources in Alberta has meant a great deal to the industrial development of that province.
On the other hand, I want to point out that the use of this fuel has meant a great deal to the mothers of families throughout our province. I am looking forward to the day when the mothers of families from the Alberta boundary to the heart of Quebec will be able to use gas to cook their meals and heat their houses. In the early days of gas exploration in Alberta, particularly after Mr. Manning took over, there was established what was called the gas export policy of that province. He insisted that so far as the use of gas was concerned, the first consideration in Alberta should be domestic use; the second concern should be the use for the development of Alberta industries; and third, the export of gas out of the province.
