3.	It is utterly ridiculous for opposition members to contend there has been inexcusable delay in making a start on the Trans-Canada project. Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited, as presently constituted, is little more than two years old. It was in January, 1954, that the original Trans-Canada company amalgamated with Western Pipe Lines Limited to present an entirely new natural gas transmission project.
It is true that the original Trans-Canada company was incorporated by this parliament in 1951. But it is equally true, and of public record, that the original Trans-Canada company failed in its objective, its proposal to build a pipe line across Canada from Alberta to Quebec which would be entirely dependent on Canadian sales. The original Trans-Canada company spent millions of dollars on gas exploration, extensive market studies and detailed engineering in a sincere effort to reach its goal but found that markets were not immediately available in Canada in sufficient volume to meet the stringent requirements of pipe line financing. Too, the government of Alberta refused to grant the original Trans-Canada company an export licence on the conviction that marketing restricted to Canada could not provide a fair return to Alberta producers.
The Alberta government was firm in its insistence that export to a substantial and readily accessible United States market be at least an integral part of any plan to take surplus gas out of that province. A new Trans-Canada company emerged from this deadlock in January, 1954, a company whose objective represented a compromise between the declared policies of the government of Canada and the government of Alberta.

From the outset, export of Canadian gas to the United States was part and parcel of the new undertaking.
Now we hear much idle talk of delays and failures on the part of Trans-Canada. What are the facts? The facts are that the new Trans-Canada company has made tremendous progress. It must not be forgotten this is to be the biggest pipe line in the world; its capital requirements far exceed those of the St. Lawrence seaway development. Its building will result in a billion dollars being spent in Canada on natural gas facilities within the next three years.
Within four months of the formation of the new company, on May 10, 1954, Trans-Canada was granted an export permit by the petroleum and natural gas conservation board of Alberta to take four trillion three hundred and fifty billion cubic feet out of Alberta in the next 25 years. This export quota represented the total estimated market requirements of Canada in that 2J decade period and enough to export 200 million cubic feet of gas daily to the United States for 25 years.
Two months later, in July 1954, Trans-Canada appeared before the board of transport commissioners in Ottawa and was granted a provisional permit to build the line across Canada and a spur south from Winnipeg to carry export gas to the Canada-United States border at Emerson, Manitoba. The permit was provisional to the degree the company still had to prove financibility.
In the same month, July 1954, Trans-Canada applied to the board of transport commissioners for a permit to build a pipe line from Niagara Falls to Toronto to bring in a temporary supply of American gas for the metropolitan Toronto area. This interim supply was important because it would temporarily satisfy a pressing need of the Consumers' Gas Company and would assist in the development of a much larger market for Alberta gas when it arrived in Toronto. This Niagara-Toronto line was started within three weeks after the transport board permit was granted, was completed three months later, and the conversion from manufactured to natural gas was in effect in Toronto by November 7, 1954. This 76-mile line cost $5,300,000 and its cost was borne by the sponsors of Trans-Canada.
Simultaneously, Trans-Canada, equipped for the first time with proper authority, embarked on vigorous purchase and sales programs, buying hundreds of billions of cubic feet of natural gas from the Alberta producers and arranging to sell it to utility companies and industries along its 2350-mile route to Montreal. Some considerable progress was made in both directions but, in
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation both cases, Trans-Canada was faced with problems beyond its control. With the exception of a section of southwestern Ontario, none of the communities along the pipe line route had used natural gas nor knew much about it. Utility companies, either public or privately-controlled, had yet to be established in most communities. Thus, in many instances, there was no second party with whom Trans-Canada could negotiate. This is still the case in many centres but most of the large market areas now have gas utility companies and have firm contracts with the pipe line company.
At the other end of the line, in Alberta, purchase contracts were lagging too; it was evident many large producers were going to hold out until they achieved strong representation of their industry within the framework of the pipe line company. This led to a broadening of the base of the Trans-Canada company to include Canadian Gulf Oil Limited, which owns one of the largest gas reservoirs in Alberta, and Hudson Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited, another major and respected gas and oil producer.
Appreciation of the extension of sponsorship was soon evident among producers. Purchase contract negotiations were speeded up; long-term agreements, favourable to both the pipe line and the producers, were much easier to negotiate. At this moment, June 5, 1956, Trans-Canada has signed purchase contracts with Alberta producers for the limit of its export permit.
In the early summer of 1955 Trans-Canada signed a contract with Tennessee Gas Transmission Company to export to this company, at the Manitoba-Minnesota border, 200 million cubic feet of gas daily for a 25-year period. The requirement of the Alberta government to export to an accessible and substantial U.S. market was met to the best of the ability of Trans-Canada. This export requires the approval of the federal power commission of the United States and it is now being considered.
By midsummer 1955, the prospect for making a start on the line in 1956 appeared quite bright. Plans were completed for the importation from the United States of additional interim supplies of gas to serve the area from Toronto to and including Montreal as a market development measure pending the arrival of Alberta gas. The necessary pipe for this line was placed on firm order and an application was made to the federal power commission of the United States for a permit to import the temporary supply. This application is also under consideration by the United States commission at this time.
As late summer, 1955, approached it was necessary to arrange for the scarce 34-inch

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation diameter steel pipe for the 575-mile line to Winnipeg. This created a real problem. The pipe would cost close to $40 million; it was in heavy demand. A firm order was required and this large amount of money-still a highly speculative risk-posed a large problem.
Read more slowly.
Not so fast.

In late October, with a November 1 deadline for the order looming, Trans-Canada decided to ask Tennessee Gas Transmission if it would consider placing the order on that company's line of credit with the steel company and, in return, assume, if it desired, a sponsoring position in Trans-Canada. Tennessee Gas agreed to the proposal, came into Trans-Canada on an equal basis with Canadian Gulf and Hudson Bay Oil and Gas, and assumed its share of the sponsoring cost of the pipe line company.
Sales contracts continued to grow in overall quantity but still fell short of the amount required to pay the fixed charges on the line, the prime requirement in pipe line financing. It soon became evident that without some form of extraordinary financial assistance, the line could not be started in 1956 and the Canadian government was advised of the problem. It was decided parliament would be asked at this session to provide assistance of assuming the responsibility of building the costly section of the line between the Mani-toba-Ontario border and Kapuskasing. At the same time, the strongest possible case was placed before the federal power commission of the United States for the important export to Minnesota, a sale which, had it been approved in time, would have made the entire project immediately economical and financi-ble. This, however, was not to be the case; the import licence was contested by other interests in the United States and the hearing is still in progress.
Meanwhile, time was running out for the 1956 construction period. At best, Trans-Canada needed 120 construction days to build the line from Alberta to Winnipeg.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are opposing third reading of this bill, as we have opposed this legislation right from the start, because we regard it as a bad deal for the people of Canada. There are on the other side of this house those who seem to have fallen for the notion that the purpose of this bill is to build

a line that will distribute gas in this country. Surely any who have studied the matter realize that the whole purpose of the promoters of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited and Tennessee Gas Transmission Company which is behind Trans-Canada is to make use of Canadian gas for the purpose of breaking into the profitable industrial market in the central and mid-western part of the United States. True, contracts have been signed as a sideline to distribute gas to some areas in western Canada, including my own city of Winnipeg; but with regard to that I simply say that it has already been made clear that the Winnipeg and Central Gas Company which expects to get gas from Trans-Canada for something of the order of 28 cents a thousand cubic feet has applied for permission to sell that gas to the consumers in Winnipeg at a price of $1.10 a thousand cubic feet. That, of course, is run-of-the-mill practice so far as a private corporation of this kind is concerned.
There are those who think that they are voting on a proposition that will eventually get gas into Ontario and perhaps into Quebec. That could happen. It might happen. But the chances are it will not. To those who have studied the matter-to those who have listened to thoughtful discussions of this matter such as that which we saw and heard on "This Week" on Sunday night over the C.B.C. -it is clear that there is a great deal of uncertainty as to whether this line will ever result in gas being brought into the eastern Canadian market. The purpose of the Tennessee company, the purpose of Trans-Canada, is to get hold of this Canadian gas so that they can use it to break into the United States industrial market and make huge profits out of this resource that belongs to the people of Canada.
There are those who dare to hope that the day will come, despite the efforts being made by the promoters of this company, that there will be a system of considerable proportions distributing gas through the various parts of Canada. If there is any hope that that realization might come about I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that that makes it all the more important that this whole project should be under public ownership and control. If the picture that has been painted for us regarding the distribution of gas in Canada is to be realized, it means that in due course some 30 per cent of the people of this nation could be concerned in this project.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that a project of that significance, a project that might concern some 30 per cent of the people of this country, should not be under foreign private ownership, should not be under private ownership

at all, but should be under the ownership and control of the Canadian people. Because this bill sets out to alienate control over this resource and over its distribution to foreign private interests, we maintain that this bill is a bad deal for the people of Canada. We in the opposition are trying our best not just to delay this bill. Let me disabuse others on the opposite side of that opinion. We do not want just to delay this bill. We are still trying to defeat it. In doing so, we are carrying out our responsibilities to the people who sent us to this free parliament.
We have heard a great deal from the other side, including many interjections from the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill), though I do not believe he has made a speech in the debate. I imagine if someone did the arithmetic involved in counting the number of times his name is on Hansard, as has been done for some of the rest of us-quite a compliment, I might say-it would be found that his name is on Hansard quite often, but he has not yet given us a speech. May I say to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and to the rest of the government, particularly to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), and there is something very pointed I want to say to him tonight, that they do not yet seem to have appreciated the fundamentals of this situation. They have made up their minds they want to put this bill through. They come before us and they talk about the will of the majority. They talk about majorities having the right to vote and decide on the issues. I want to deal with that in terms of what I call the fundamentals in just a moment. Before I do so may I indicate just how this decision of the so-called majority was reached. It is set out very clearly for us on page 202 of "The Canadian Liberal", for the first quarter of 1956. This is certainly an official publication because the editorial advisory board is headed by D. K. MacTavish, Q.C., who seems to head a great many things. On page 202 I find a part of the speech which was made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) at that Liberal banquet which was held earlier this year. He said:
I heard a song a while ago entitled "What Lola wants Lola gets". But the point about all this is that when the decision is made, when the Prime Minister says, "This is the course we will take", Mr. Gardiner follows the party line without the slightest deviation. There is never a word expressed outside the council chamber that he had ever had a different point of view about the matter at issue.
In other words, this decision of the majority that the Prime Minister and the rest of the
1956	4731
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation cabinet tell us must be accepted by parliament is a decision that was first of all made in the cabinet on the basis of that slogan, "What Lola wants, Lola gets".
Now, Mr. Speaker, apart from Lola let me get down to fundamentals. We have heard references in this debate to the British North America Act and Magna Carta. May I remind those who may be quoting the British North America Act that section 50 provides for parliament to remain in office for not more than five years. Section 50 does not say that every elected parliament must remain here five years. No, it allows a parliament to last not more than five years, subject to being sooner dissolved by the governor general. What is the fundamental proposition involved in section 50 of the British North America Act? It is that we have what is known as responsible government. It is different from government in some other countries where a congress or an elected legislature is elected for a set period of time. We have responsible government which is based on the proposition that the government has the constitutional right to go ahead and put legislation through parliament only so long as it has the confidence and support of the majority of the electorate of this country.

Our aim, Mr. Speaker, is to defeat this bill and we hope that even yet the arguments that we are permitted to make in the next three hours and five minutes will persuade the government that it is trying to foist upon the people of Canada a bad bill.
Last evening the Minister of Finance paid me the compliment of suggesting that I had spoken more than 30 times in this debate. I do not mind that reference, but just to keep the record straight-and I suppose this will produce a bit of humour, but let us have the record straight-this is only the second time that I have actually spoken in this debate itself. All of the other times that I have risen to my feet-and it may be 28 other times or even 50 times-have been on points of order, and I make no apology for doing my best to persuade this parliament that it is not only important to get things done; it is important to do them in the right way.
I wish to point out, Mr. Speaker, that during the course of this legislation there have been a number of instances of what we regard as the breaking of the rules of this House of Commons. It is not my purpose in reciting them at this moment, or reciting just a few of them, at any rate, to argue each case over again. The house has made its decision, but I think we should have a catalogue of what has been done by this government. First of all, a second resolution was put on the order paper when an earlier resolution was already there. We fought that three different times because we felt it was wrong. Then, skipping over some of the minor infractions of the rules, we reached the occasion when, in my view, the government sought to go beyond what was included in standing order 33, the first night we were met with closure, when it brought in the bill the same night the resolution was passed. The government also broke a fundamental rule and presented parliament with a gross insult when it gave us a bill without the agreement attached to it which is referred

In due course, we got into committee and we had the Minister of Trade and Commerce, imposing, even before official closure under standing order 33, a form of closure that he devised-unless the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration suggested it to him-that of postponing discussion on the first three clauses, with the result that the only clause we discussed in committee was clause 4. In that connection, since the Prime Minister is fond of reading Redlich, an ancient authority, may I ask him to read a page other than the one he read yesterday. I refer him to page 92, paragraph 3, which reads:
We may, then, say that the centre of gravity of the whole legislative action of the House of Commons lies in the region of the work of committee of the whole house. It is in committee that the fate of a bill is really decided; its ultimate form is there settled in the clash of parties and opinions or by the compromises made between them. In this stage debate is quite free: members may speak to each question as often as necessary.
Over on page 93 Redlich says this:
The rules provide, of course, for the application of the closure to debate in committee as well as in the house. It may be moved and carried upon every question before the committee. But its use in committee, except sparingly, is regarded as unwarrantable conduct on the part of the majority. All opinions ought here to have an opportunity of free expression.
That is Redlich, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's authority, used by him in another debate. I suggest that he read these pages and realize how grave is the sin that he has committed in asking this parliament to give third reading tonight to a bill which, when it was in committee of the whole, was discussed, so far as this house was concerned, only with regard to one clause because we had this vicious form of closure, not only the application of standing order 33 in a way which I feel was in violation of the rules, following the bad precedent of 1932, but we had this other form of closure that the Minister of Trade and Commerce introduced right from the start. That, I say, Mr. Speaker, is in violation of the basic principles laid down in Redlich as well as in other authorities.
I see that my time is running out. I will not be able to complete the catalogue of the rules that have been broken; but, Mr. Speaker, let me say this to you. What has happened throughout this debate? It is not just so much that an individual standing order, an individual rule, an individual citation here and there has been broken; the terrible result is that there has been built up an over-all precedent, an over-all fact that this parliament can never forget; not just that the rules can be broken, but the precedent that has been established in this debate is that
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation parliament can be made to bow to the will of one man. If it has been done once, as it has, it can be done again. No pipe line is worth it.
I conclude with these words. I direct them to the Prime Minister in the hope that even yet, between now and one o'clock tonight, he will reconsider this matter and tell these men behind him who do not want an election that this whole matter is too serious, and take it to the country.
We want gas in Winnipeg.

I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and through you to the Prime Minister, what shall it profit Canada if we gain a pipe line and lose this nation's soul? Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I have risen to take part in this debate on the pipe line but I thought I could devote a few moments to dealing with the beneficial effect that the construction of this pipe line would have on Canada. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) said that this would mean the expenditure in Canada of about $1 billion which would include the capital cost of the construction of the pipe line, the capital cost of the distribution of the gas plus the capital cost of assembling and purifying the gas.
In my county of Welland a new company, the Welland Tubes Limited, has been formed as a subsidiary of the Steel Company of Canada and of the Page-Hersey Tubes, Limited. This company is presently building a plant five acres in extent to make 30-inch pipe to build a part of the line from Winnipeg to Montreal. In fact, it has already been announced by Trans-Canada Limited that this company will be awarded a $45 million contract for 30-inch pipe. They should be in operation early in the new year. Besides this, Page-Hersey Tubes, Limited', will be making much of the pipe required in the smaller subsidiary lines necessary for the distribution of gas.
The total length of the pipe line from Alberta to Montreal is about 2200 miles. The 

pipe for the 34-inch line from Alberta to Winnipeg will be supplied by United States companies at a cost of about $40 million. The 30-inch pipe for the distance from Winnipeg to Montreal will be supplied by British and Canadian firms. The British share is $32 million and the share of the Canadian firm is $45 million or 60 per cent of the 30-inch line. This is' a very sizeable order indeed for a company which has the know-how but as yet has no buildings and no machinery, or at least not much machinery for building pipe of this size.
I am impressed with the capable management of Page-Hersey Tubes, Limited, and no doubt they will direct this project. I know many of their men and I feel confident that they are admirably qualified in a technical way to build this pipe.
Ever since the pipe line was proposed I have been in constant touch with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I want to thank the minister for saying he would do his best to see that all the pipe that could be made in Canada for this project would be obtained here. I think the minister has been most fair. He has always been out to help Canadian industry and when he has kept Canadian industry at work he has maintained employment at a high level.
Before departing on his trip to Australia I called to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce the fact that the Atlas Steels company of Welland was somewhat slack. This has opened up a new market for this company in that part of the world and I would express the hope that they can continue to get sufficient nickel to fill their expanding export markets.

The manufacturing of pipe will be a year-round operation. Many workmen experienced in various technical skills will be employed and this will help alleviate the condition of seasonal unemployment in the wintertime. The manufacture of this pipe in Welland will help to boom the economy of Welland

Much has been said about the rules of the house. I agree that we must have rules of procedure and that these must be based on decisions of the past, but too many rules, many of which seem to conflict, to my mind tend to make our democratic processes inefficient. We should strive to make them effective and dynamic. I think we should be able to contrive rules that would leave protection with the minority but at the same time afford rights to the majority, who in the final analysis must take the responsibility of government. After all, it is the differentiation of these rights that comes into play in the procedure of closure.
Our mother of parliaments at Westminster conducts its business much more expeditiously than we do here. I understand that closure is used there as often as 22 times a session. True, it is more often by agreement, but forced closure does occur as occasion requires. But agreement on closure is more readily arrived at when there is a suggestion of forced closure behind it.
I think that if our parliament is to have the confidence of the people we should be spending more time on the business for which we were sent here rather than on long procedural debates. Repetition of argument on succeeding stages of a bill, particularly by the same speaker, is inexcusable, since it is time consuming and costs the taxpayers money. Some hon. members in this house seem to think that there is something wrong with the application of closure. Even the Prime Minister said it was distasteful to him, but he is to be admired for going through with it when it is for the good of the Canadian people as a whole. The Conservative party has used it two or three times this generation. Now we have used it, supported by the Social Credit party. I think the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis) speaking for the C.C.F., said the other night that it should be used on occasion.
Why then the outcry when approximately three-quarters of the members in attendance in this house have been consistently voting for this pipe-line bill? Under these conditions, would any reasonable, disinterested person say that the bill should not pass? Majorities rule in all western democracies; minorities rule behind the iron curtain and in those parts of the world where tyranny still exists. Why should a minority rule here?

It is time that some sanity returned to this house. The Prime Minister is both gracious and generous. He is too much of a gentleman to reply in kind. Some three weeks have passed now since the government started its plan of muzzling parliament and since it adopted a new type of closure, which is a type of foreclosure to prevent disclosure. One question which has been asked and which has not been answered by the Prime Minister or any of the other ministers is this, and I again throw the challenge out to the government to answer it When in all parliamentary history has this course ever been followed before of adopting closure before discussion begins? I have perused the records of parliament, the history of Britain; I have taken the records of closure during the years; and in large measure it has been imposed as a result of agreement. I can find no trace where in the mother of parliaments such a course was adopted whereby parliament was frustrated from discussion by reason of the actions of the Prime Minister and those associated with him.
As I listened to my hon. friend, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), last evening, I enjoyed hearing a parliamentary speech made in parliamentary style and I compliment him for that speech. I say to him that he did not answer that question; he evaded that question. History shows that Gerry, the governor of one of the states, finally achieved the unusual distinction of having his name used in connection with gerrymander. Another politician, Roorback, achieved the doubtful distinction of having his name associated, by reason of his conduct, with false and frivolous stories a few days in advance of an election when it was too late to deny them. My hon. friend, the Minister of Finance, too has achieved immortality in having created what I think in future years will be known as the Harris closure, whereby the mouths of parliament are silenced in advance because of the fear of the government that disclosures would defeat the purposes of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I am one of those-and there are many of us-who love parliament. The House of Commons-with its traditions, its dedication to preserve and maintain freedom, its necessary dependence on the fact that an opposition

As you know, Mr. Speaker, being about to publish a book on the subject of the rules of parliament, the rules of parliament should not be altered, dare not be changed in order to meet the demands of an overwhelming majority. Only yesterday the Prime Minister, in the course of his speech giving one of the reasons for the action the other day which denied the rights of parliament, when the decision of the previous day was reversed in the morning, said that after all that prejudiced the government. I have his exact words, and I asked him to repeat them. "To the prejudice of the government." Is that the basis upon which parliament is operating? Is that the basis by which we in fact, as members of this house, are to be attendants at the will of the Prime Minister and those associated with him? Sir, the events of the last week will be forgotten, but not forgotten in this generation will be the short-cuts through freedom that have been made by a government that has set the zero hour and then curtailed the rights of parliament in order to achieve an arbitrary date. Was it not a fact that a year ago he was opposed to advancing money to this corporation? Was it not a fact that a year ago he did not wish to guarantee the bonds of this corporation? He nods assent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, act your age, John.

He has dominated parliament. Having dominated parliament, are we to say that in the lesser sphere of party politics it would not be beneficial to those who have ambition to have him within their corner? Yes, I ask that, for I find it passing difficult to understand why the Minister of Finance should have deemed it necessary to alter his direction, to change his viewpoint in a matter of a few months. The company that for five years broke every promise, that denied the achievement of everything it advanced, suddenly became even in the mind of the Minister of Finance a puppet equal in favour to the favour it enjoyed in the mind of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Why the change? In order to achieve a temporary victory, the victory of the opportunity of a

majority to say "yes", every right of parliament has been mercilessly and brutally mutilated. Yes, Mr. Speaker, your book is out of date even before it is published.
And we have had all of that in but a few weeks, all of that in order to achieve the glory of a victory that depends upon evasion of the rules. Why, Mr. Speaker, can you imagine how the rules have been perverted when today becomes yesterday because, as the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said, otherwise it would have prejudiced the government? Oh, it is a dreadful picture. It is one that the members of this government will hear about, it is one about which the Canadian people are beginning to realize what my hon. friend who just took his seat so emphasized, the need of efficiency. Has that not been the cry of every dictator and every potential dictator in every generation? Parliament works too slowly. They want action now. The rules have been with us for generations. Dump out the rules. Evade them. Place Mr. Speaker in an unenviable position, having established the apex of authority and prestige.
Surely, sir, never in the history of this parliament has there been such sordid action to place Mr. Speaker in a position whereby all of the things for which he stood are to be subverted to the temporary desires of an immediate victory, of a fixed date. Oh, it is quite a picture. It is one that governments in the years ahead will look back upon and their members will say: Was that Liberalism in 1956?

November 23, 1955
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation

A simple perusal of this document indicates as follows. My leader yesterday placed on record the figures for the period from November 1, 1957 to November 1, 1958 and so on year by year. In every year until 1962 Canadians are going to pay on the wholesale price approximately 7 cents to 10 cents more per thousand cubic feet than will the Americans. The Midwestern company, of course, is in a dual position.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext: Time.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext: Mr. Gardiner Symonds is in the position of being a director and one of the bosses of Trans-Canada. He is also the head of Midwestern because it is a subsidiary of Tennessee. He buys cheaply from the Canadian organization and he sells at extremely high prices in the United States. My right hon. friend says that these were phony figures. The only thing phony about them was that they were given by Trans-Canada Pipe Lines corporation before the federal power commission of the United States. I make this suggestion. If they are right-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext: I am glad you put in that qualification, "if they are right".

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext:
Yes, I say "if they are right". If they are right my right hon. friend, regardless of what the law may be in Canada, is actually helping a corporation to soak Canadians for the benefit of these very desirable promoters, these adventurers from Texas trading into Canada, and away with Canada's resources. On the other hand, if they are false,-and I want to be fair to my right hon. friend because it is his suggestion that they are-may I say that they are the only figures that this company has presented before the federal power commission of the United States. If they are false, the Trans-Canada officers and officials are trying to obtain, by false pretences, an order of a United States commission. I do not care which alternative you take. On the one hand, they are defrauding Canada, if you believe that the figures are correct; and they are certainly in the evidence of Mr. Low, the sales manager. If they are false, the purpose is to delude a United States commission into believing-in order to secure an order from the United States of America- that the price will be advantageous to the United States.
That is the kind of thing that we wanted to have before a committee, Mr. Speaker. The government say they gave us the right to speak, the right to question. In committee, when we asked one question after closure, we were out. We lost our position. We could not follow up. We wanted to see that
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation benign and benevolent man, Mr. Gardiner Symonds. We desired to have an opportunity of finding out how he, on the one hand, as a director of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, would be able to secure the best price for Canadians and how, as the motivating genius of the Tennessee company and the Midwestern company, he would at the same time be desiring to secure the lowest possible price. Mr. Speaker, the record is there. The Minister of Trade and Commerce the other day was obliged to rise and say to my friend the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Michener), "If my figures are right"; because he pointed out that on the figures given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, Canadians were being mulcted for the benefit of the people of the United States. He said, "If it is right,
I will stop it; I will use the law". What have you been doing?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext: Nothing.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext: Confession is good for the soul, even in the dying days of a debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext: There has been no gas export permit issued.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext:
That is exactly what the minister has been doing, nothing, but endeavouring to railroad through the House of Commons legislation for a company the desirability of whose claim is subject to the most serious suspicion. Certainly, there should have been a most serious examination.
Sir, I should like to have dealt with the McMahon plan. I should like to have some of the ministers conduct a little Gallup poll of their own. How many of them saw the McMahon plan?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext: We have seen lots of Gallup polls.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext: What about the Minister of Mines? I never saw it. There were only three copies and the minister had three and they were all private and confidential. I put it to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that he told McMahon to write "private and confidential" on there. McMahon produced the record and the minister said write "private and confidential"-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext: At times it has been frenzied. It was forecast many years ago, the tactics that should be followed by a Conservative opposition in such a discussion.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext: That was when you were a Tory.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext:
I can stand heckling, but' I do not like to be insulted in that way. A great Canadian, Mr. Speaker, the late John W. Dafoe, in his book "Clifford Sifton in Relation to his Times", had this to say in describing the tactics of the opposition of 1897 to a railway bill introduced by Mr. Sifton. From his book I quote the following paragraphs which have a peculiar relationship to the debate we have been having in this house. He said:
If any Canadian satirist wishes to write an oration for the use of an opposition resisting a government proposition to build or assist in building a railway-
Or, if you like, a pipe line.
-he can readily find his material in that vast repository of talk, the Canadian Hansard. The lines of the attack are defined by usage and sanctified by tradition.
This was written many years ago.
First it must be urged that the building of the road is too early or too late . . . then the route is 

all wrong; it either starts at the wrong place or follows the wrong course. The parties to whom the building of the road-
Or the pipe line.
-is given are not the right parties.
Then, Mr. Dafoe put in quotes some of his own reflections on this.
"Is not the government aware, Mr. Speaker, that the bankers of London, New York, Paris and Kalamazoo, in alliance with the engineers of Great Britain, the United States, Germany and Kamschatka are eager to build this railway, and given the opportunity are prepared to make a proposition which will save this country millions and rescue the people from the hands of the exploiters whom the government delight to honour?"
Then, Mr. Dafoe went on:
Since the government cannot tear up the contract any alternative offer can be put in the most attractive light; while conversely, the arrangement, to which the government is committed, is to be painted in the darkest colours. Flagitious, corrupt, improvident, perfidious, knavish, faithless are words very suitable to be used. Any member of the opposition can be trusted to say that the treasury of the country is being robbed in order that means may be obtained for the debauching of the electors;-

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext: That is obvious.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext:
I continue the quotation:
-but only those most skilful in the art of innuendo should be permitted to hint that there is a private and sinister explanation of the favouritism displayed by the minister. By the use of some such formula an opposition running to interminable length can be offered.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the opposition has undoubtedly run to an interminable length, but there has not been as much discussion on the bill during this interminable length as on things external to the bill. This is probably a good reason why the Minister of External Affairs should take part.
The opposition, of course, claim, and they claim very often, to be gagged. If that is true, Mr. Speaker, they are the noisiest group of gagged men in history. They have talked, gag or no gag, endlessly on the bill, around the bill, above the bill and below the bill. They have ranged far and wide from Alcibiades, through Shakespeare down to poor old Guy Fawkes and then on to Hitler. They have raised endless points of order, questions of privilege, especially from one or two members.
A charge, and it is a serious one, has been levelled that what we are witnessing in this debate is the end of our parliamentary freedom.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext: Well, that is the charge, Mr. Speaker.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext: Absolutely right.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext: What in reality are exaggerated and excitable statements cannot destroy the facts any more than carefully contrived scenes in the House of Commons can obscure them. Parliamentary government is in danger when the government elected in a democratic way is prevented from carrying on the business of government by a minority using and exploiting the rules of the house. To prevent that, Mr. Speaker-

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext: What about closure?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE
speechtext: I wonder if some of the apostles of free speech would allow me to continue my speech. To prevent this, there are rules of closure recognized in every deliberative assembly, and in most of them the rules are far stricter than they are in this assembly. That rule has been applied here, not to stop debate but to limit it. In that connection, reference has been made very often to the use of closure in the mother of parliaments, about which we have heard so much in the discussion. Let us see what happens in the parliament at Westminster. From 1945 to 1951, which was the period when the Socialist government was in power in the United Kingdom, the maximum time actually devoted to the consideration of any government money bill by the House of Commons during that period of six years was 21 hours and 25 minutes.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED-ESTIMATED ANNUAL SALES AND REVENUE

including 44 minutes on the resolution preceding the bill, 7 hours and 18 minutes were given to second reading, 10 hours in committee, 22 minutes on the report and 2 hours and 35 minutes on third reading.

spent in debate on a bill over there during that parliament was 4 hours and 44 minutes That country, Mr. Speaker, the home of parliamentary freedom, also understands the necessities of parliamentary government, the responsibilities and rights of the government as well as of the opposition.

As my hon. friend the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) pointed out tonight, this is not a debate on a pipe line bill as such. That was authorized five years ago. Those things were sanctioned by parliament and the franchise was granted by the Department of Transport five years ago. What we are considering tonight is not the operation of a pipe line as such but the financing of it by this parliament, which is an entirely different thing. What we are considering tonight is the-

We are considering the fact that having authorized the franchise of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited five year? ago, and that company having made application to the board of transport commissioners and all the rest of it, we are now asked to provide the money for the project. Someone has said that we the opposition, the C.C.F. and this group, are delaying this matter- after five years!
Where are we tonight, Mr. Speaker? We are asked to provide the money. We started out presumably to build the so-called bridge across northern Ontario. We moved from that and now we have to loan millions of dollars for the construction of that portion of the line which these entrepreneurs, when they came before us five years ago, said was the easiest part. They said it presented no difficulties whatsoever and as a matter of fact neither did the northern Ontario line because even if the northern Ontario section cost more, think how cheap it was to build the line across the prairies and they could average the two. On the basis of those assurances the committee of this parliament and the board of transport commissioners gave authority to them to go ahead and now we are facing this situation tonight. It is really a ludicrous situation in many ways, because, as the member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out, the pipe line has already been authorized, and as appeared in the press tonight from the pen of a distinguished Canadian columnist there is going to be lots
4746	HOUSE OF
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation of gas to be transported in this country; we are simply laying the foundation of how it is to be transported and it is a most unfortunate thing that in this we should have bogged down in the way we have.
Why have we done it? Because before this measure came before parliament the executive saw fit to enter into an agreement whereby they said this shall be done by June 7. There was no reference to consulting parliament in the agreement or the passing of legislation by parliament. The executive said, this shall be done by June 7, and that was the thing with which this parliament was confronted when this bill first came into the house. I can say, without any fear of contradiction, there has never been a more indecent form of closure imposed upon any parliament in the world than that in the form of the agreement entered into by the executive with the United States tycoons before the executive brought legislation into the house.
I think I can say this. I notice the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) is not here at the moment, but I think I can say this as one Baptist to another. This Machiavellian Baptist on the other side of the house now says, "Well, my friend from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) said in a radio broadcast-

Those are not the reasons why closure was imposed; they have nothing to do with it. Closure was inevitable once this government, behind the backs of parliament and with no consultation with it, went ahead and entered into this agreement whereby June 7 became the date of execution by parliament. Make no mistake about that. They tied the hands of this parliament. When they hide behind certain indirect statements or direct statements which may have been made, then it simply shows the weakness of the case.
That is the only reason why we have closure at this time. My hon. friend, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) once said he had a crystal ball into which he gazes from time to time. Probably he gazed into the crystal ball and saw there was going to be some resistance to this in parliament. And why should there not be? If the opposition realizes its responsibilities, why should there not be? In addition to whatever may be said about the bridge across northern Ontario, we are called upon to lend $80 million to United states entrepreneurs so that they may build a


pipe line across Canada whereby they can carry Canadian gas into the United States. That is the situation.
There have been many United States visitors sitting in the galleries in the past few days, and I hope there are some sitting here now. The other day a friend of mine was sitting in the gallery, and one of them was sitting alongside him. He was asking what this fight was all about. My friend said, "It is a question of a bill whereby the government of Canada is asking to borrow money whereby it can finance a company that is 83 per cent United States controlled to build a pipe line whereby Canadian gas ultimately can go into the United States." The American replied, "If they had the sense that God gave geese, they would be opposed to that." I think that is common sense. That is why some of this debate has gone on in the way in which it has.
Much has been said about the fact that there have been 14 days of debate. The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) dealt with that today. The time that has been given to the debate on this pipe line per se has been very much restricted. No one knows it better than my friends over here, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, who have a knowledge of history and some understanding of what I mean. If they had been sitting in this opposition-

I wonder what the Secretary of State for External Affairs would have said about this if he had been sitting here. I can imagine the fulminations, the speeches he could have made about this horrible, atrocious thing that a government was doing at this time and under these circumstances. That is why, when they talk for 14 days or 16 days or whatever it may have been, the opposition has been trying to develop, during the latter part of this debate at any rate, the rights of parliament itself. Those are much more important than the pipe line itself, important as it may be.
Why are we facing this step tonight? We were told from the beginning that there was a great need for haste. We were told that the steel necessary for pipe might be sold to the Arabians or somewhere else, that it was in such short supply that unless the parliament of Canada passed this bill by June 7 Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited might lose that steel. That was the only argument that has ever been advanced, as far as I can remember, for the passage of this bill.
Yet what did we hear this afternoon? What did we hear from the Minister of Finance? He said that for 14 or 16 days, or whatever

the number of days may have been, the government had been urging that the bill had to be passed because there might be a shortage of steel, but perhaps they were wrong and perhaps, looking at the economic situation, there would not be any shortage of steel. Perhaps there is going to be a depression; perhaps there is going to be unemployment. He suggested that there might be a surplus rather than a shortage of steel, that there might be unemployment rather than full employment and therefore we should pass this bill to provide employment for Canadians who might be otherwise unemployed if by chance there is a surplus instead of a shortage of steel. I suppose the minister has been so close to the United States entrepreneurs who have said, "Heads I win; tails you lose", that he said that if he could not be right in one way he would be right in the other. If they said there was going to be a shortage of steel and then there was a surplus; if they said there was going to be a tight employment situation and then there was a need for employment; the legislation should still be passed.
I wonder just what the government intended. I wonder what the Prime Minister thinks. A few moments ago the Secretary of State for External Affairs referred to this government as headed by the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister is one for whom all of us have a great deal of liking and had a great deal of respect, but I hold in my hand a statement from the Winnipeg Free Press with respect to that gentleman heading this government. I can quite understand why he has sat nebulously quiet, why like a chameleon he shifted from one colour to another and said nothing and did nothing. Apparently the government itself did not know what it was doing or what it was going to do. This is by Mr. Grant Dexter who certainly is no Conservative. Referring to this debate in the last few days, he said this in the Winnipeg Free Press.
Through all of this hubbub, the most arresting figure on the government side of the house was Prime Minister St. Laurent. He sat, impassive, expressionless, chin in hand, an open book on his desk, silent.

were 50 closures agreed to. I point out, Mr. Speaker, that it seems there was a sudden rise after the Churchill government took office. There were also ten closures not agreed to, or a total of 60. In the 1952-53 session, from November 4, 1952 to October 29, 1953 there were 20 closures by agreement and seven closures not agreed to, a total of 27. In the 1953-54 session, from November 3, 1953, to November 25, 1954 there were 23 closures by agreement and 7 not agreed to, a total of 30. Finally, in the 1954-55 session, from November 30, 1954 to May 6, 1955 there were six by agreement and four not agreed to or a total of ten.
For the seven years there is a total of 148 by agreement and 45 not agreed to, or a grand total of 193. Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation Since we have heard many great authorities on parliamentary procedure, Mr. Speaker, I want to place on the record a very humble authority, no one of any great distinction particularly. Now, sir, I suggest to you that any government, having been told months before that there was going to be vigorous opposition to one of their measures, if that government had the slightest consideration of the decencies, the rights and properties of parliament, they would have seen fit to bring this measure in as soon as possible.
What happened? On January 10 it was foreshadowed in the speech from the throne. Then, we heard no more about it for almost a month. On February 6 a resolution was placed on the order paper. Then again it was put on ice for more than a month, about five weeks. Finally this resolution was brought before the house on March 15 and debated briefly at that time. Then on May 9-nearly two months had again elapsed before they brought this measure that they are so anxious to pass and for which there is so little time to debate-they brought it back to us. Then, they complain because in the 18 sitting days much of the time has been taken up by procedural disputes. I suggest to them that Dr. Arthur Beauchesne probably realizes the real nature of that fight. It was a fight to preserve the rights, the dignities and proprieties of parliament. This has been a fraudulent argument presented to the Canadian people deliberately to deceive them into believing that the opposition was given plenty of time but through sheer obstructionism were blocking discussion of this bill, when the record shows that this government had this measure in mind as far back as January 10. They

delayed for a month before putting it on the order paper; they delayed another five weeks before finally bringing it up for discussion, and then they delayed for two months before bringing it before parliament. However, I hope that in my speech tonight 1 shall not indulge in any personalities and that I will not arouse the heat that might have been aroused earlier in the debate.
In the earlier part of the debate, Mr. Speaker,
I have been impressed with the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Nickle). From the time that he came to this house the hon. member for Calgary South gave evidence that he was probably the best informed member in the House of Commons on oil and gas issues, and he was recognized as such in all parts of the house. His opinions were valued by the colleagues who sit in his

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation group, but recently a change has taken place in the attitudes of his colleagues. During the course of his remarks, the hon. member for Calgary South pointed out to hon. members the many new discoveries of gas and oil which have taken place in the province of Alberta. He has explained to the house that year after year a great surplus of gas and oil has been piling up in the province of Alberta, on account of lack of markets, at the average rate of 4,000,000,000 cubic feet a year. It is his estimate that $150 million has been invested by Canadians and foreign investors to explore, to investigate and to develop wells producing high-value oil and the resultant amount of gas. The $150 million which has been invested by those Canadian and foreign investors is now carrying interest which is not only a great burden to the larger companies but is also pressing some of the smaller companies.
Last year I had the personal privilege of going to the northern part of Alberta and while I was there I was flown into the Pembina oil fields. I had the opportunity of standing there and seeing one of the derricks erected. I saw some of the wells that were in operation, and on one corner of this particular field we saw a head of gas probably 15 feet to 20 feet high. I said to the engineer in charge: "What are you doing there?" He said: "We are burning off the surplus gas because we have no way of exporting it to eastern Canada. We are burning each day in this particular spot enough gas to heat the city of Toronto for one day." It is my submission, Mr. Speaker, that this country cannot afford to expend energy; to waste a valuable commodity for any great period of time. I say we should proceed with this scheme because each year that passes $25 million more is required to build the line.
This bill proposes a short-term federal loan of $80 million at 5 per cent for 90 per cent of the cost of the construction of the trans-Canada pipe line to Winnipeg. It is admitted that Alberta has a great surplus of gas. They have realized within the last year or two that there is no fear of shortage. Premier Manning has now issued a permit to export 584 million cubic feet of gas a day.
I think we must see that this surplus is used, that it is not sealed up in the earth or, worse, burned off as is being done in the situation I alluded to a moment ago. We are told the city of Winnipeg needs gas badly and must have it this year. Ontario needs gas. Because of the great industrial expansion we have had in Ontario in the last 15 years we have a need for greater energy in the banner province of Canada. I think I am permitted a licence to make that statement

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation because I come from that province. We have shown great industrial expansion in Ontario and have used up to a great extent our electrical energy and we now must turn to other sources of energy.

We think there has never been, since the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the great opportunity to do an outstanding job for our country as there is at present.

Again at page 390, Mr. Frost, speaking in the Ontario legislature, had this to say:
Undoubtedly, northern Ontario was benefiting, as undoubtedly was our province generally, since we represent half the industry of Canada and have one-third the population. Obviously Ontario should not back away from a proposition of that sort. I do not think we could afford to do business that way.

I should like to refer to a meeting held at Niagara Falls, Ontario, on May 25 last. This meeting was addressed by the Hon. Dana Porter, treasurer of the province of Ontario. The meeting was reported in the May 26 edition of the Toronto Daily Star the day following the meeting and the Toronto Star reports the meeting in this manner:
Mr. Porter stood flatly behind the Liberal government in Ottawa and took a position opposite to that of the national Progressive Conservative leader, George Drew on the subsidization of U.S. interests to construct the trans-Canada pipe line.
Mr. Porter was further quoted as saying, and I cite his words:
As a provincial government we are satisfied that a supply of natural gas is essential to the exploitation of the future and we feel that a delay of that supply would be a detriment to our own success.

Mr. Speaker, if these are the opinions of the premier of Ontario and his provincial treasurer-men who have good knowledge of this matter and I am sure they must have -then I believe it is right that this government co-operating with them should see that opportunity is given to extend the western leg of this line.
Later in his address at Niagara Falls, Mr. Porter pointed out that the 30-inch pipe line will carry energy equivalent to 8 million tons of coal and the very nature and quality of the fuel makes it of great value, particularly to the province of Ontario. Well, Mr. Speaker, that is why the premier of Ontario and his government are ready to put up $35 million for the northern leg of the pipe line which extends across the northern part of our province. They are willing to extend the time under which the arrangement could be made in order that we could provide that line. We must be ready next spring to join in a partnership with the province of Ontario in order that we can assist them to do this job. It should be borne in mind that Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited has already provided $14 million and they will provide another $7J million which will boost their total investment in this enterprise to $21 million.
I have mentioned the words of Premier Frost with regard to northern Ontario. This line will pass through such centres as Kenora, Port Arthur and Fort William, Timmins, Kapuskasing, Kirkland Lake and North Bay. Here a great industrial development awaits the people of northern Ontario and the domestic users as well will have the opportunity of using this gas. They will have a fuel which will substitute for a fuel which they now import from the state of Pennsylvania in the United States of America and they will get it at a lower cost.
So far as southern Ontario is concerned the line has already been built. From the Niagara river at Queenston crossing the counties of Lincoln, Wentworth, Halton, Peel, York and extending into the city of Toronto, Tennessee gas is flowing through a pipe line that was laid last summer. This gas is being purchased by the Consumers Gas Company of the city of Toronto for use by consumers in the city of Toronto and other consumers along the way in Niagara Falls, Welland, Grimsby and Hamilton. It is the intention of this company to block up the pipe line at the international boundary in the Niagara river and bring in Alberta gas from the opposite direction when the remainder of the line is completed. I am sure the citizens of Canada will agree that due haste should be taken to see that at the earliest possible

moment in this great industrial sector of Ontario we are using Alberta gas rather than Tennessee gas.
On May 21 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) spoke in this house and I was impressed with the fact that he felt great expenditures would take place in the development of the project. The building of the line itself, installations in consumers' homes, installations of equipment in industry and installations in various municipalities will run to over $1 billion in the next five years. If this gas is to be capped and used -and I am sure that it will-and if the companies sell their product at a profit-and I am sure that they will-then the federal treasury will profit to the extent of about 45 per cent of the profits received.
Those of us who live in the Niagara peninsula have already realized the business developments in that area. The hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan), speaking in this house earlier this evening, has pointed out to you that Page-Hersey Tubes have already a $10 million mill under construction. They propose to manufacture pipe for 150 miles of line from Sarnia to Port Credit. In addition to that, Welland Tubes Limited will manufacture the 30-inch pipe for the nothern Ontario section of this line. This cannot help giving employment not only to these particular industries but to other subsidiary industries in that area, and it will mean that industries coming into that area will provide a great impetus to business in the whole Niagara frontier.
During the course of this debate and in the newspapers of the country, we have heard a great deal about closure in the past few days. I think that a number of our people are of the opinion that we have closed the mouths of the opposition members. Members have said in this house that they have been gagged, that freedom of expression is at an end, that parliament has died. Those are some of the expressions that have been used. Last evening I thought I would look at the record of the proceedings in the house since May 10 last.
Yesterday the Minister of Finance made certain statements regarding the time expended by certain particular members. I have not counted those figures but I know that this house has been in session on this debate for 17 days. During those 17 days, up to last evening-and I think that during the course of the debate today honours have been fairly well divided-the members of the official opposition party have spoken 82 times, and members of the C.C.F. group have spoken 58 times, for a total of those in opposition to this measure of 140 speeches. Mr. Knowles raised a point of order to the effect that, when the motion for third reading of the bill had been disposed of, the terms of the motion adopted in this sitting had been met; and since the motion "That the said bill do now pass and the title be as on the order paper" was a distinctly separate question, it could not be taken after the ordinary hour of adjournment.
I ruled that the motion "That the bill do now pass and the title be as on the order paper" was votable, but since it was a formal procedural motion connected with the question for third reading, it must be decided forthwith, in accordance with the terms of standing order 33; whereupon Mr. Knowles appealed to the house from my ruling.
